summary: Redwood ran through Optimize console recommendations focused on batching and caching tradeoffs for Quarry Data's conversational assistant. Discussed prefix vs session/KV caching, TTL and hit-rate expectations, latency SLOs, and cost model scenarios for hosted vs dedicated deployments. Customer requested a 48-hour benchmark and vendor security docs; next step is a POC kickoff and pricing sheet for dedicated capacity.
topics: Cache strategy: prefix cache vs KV/session cache
Cost modeling for hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment
transcript:
[00:00] Avery (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining. we planned about 45 minutes, we'll walk through the optimize console recommendations and then leave time for Qs.
[00:12] Maya (Quarry): yep thanks, appreciate it. ran into some scheduling but we're good.
[00:20] Diego (Redwood SE): quick note, i'll take the deep parts on batching and the sim results, avery will cover pricing and next steps.
[00:30] Tom (Quarry): sounds good. to set context — we're running a conversational assistant, hybrid infra: some on-prem for PII, most traffic lives in us-west cloud. our 95th p95 latency target is ~200ms tail we try to keep p99 under 400 if possible.
[00:52] Sara (Quarry): and cost's a big deal — we have a monthly token budget that's pretty tight.
[01:04] Avery: perfect — so we'll focus on two levers: batching (concurrency and batch size) and caching (prefix cache vs KV/session cache), and how those affect your per-token cost vs tail latency.
[01:18] Maya: quick q: we were looking at Redwood Dedicated earlier — how different is the econ from hosted api?
[01:26] Avery: short answer: dedicated gives predictable unit cost and lower per-token for sustained traffic; hosted is faster to spin up but higher marginal. you'll see numbers in the pricing sheet. dedicated also gives isolated GPU pools and easier compliance controls.
[01:40] Tom: we have some strict data residency. would dedicated mean we can lock it into our VPC?
[01:47] Diego: yes — Dedicated + Private deployment options allow VPC peering and customer-controlled networking, and the private control plane option supports on-prem air-gapped installs with KMS. there are operational differences that matter for latency and autoscaling.
[02:03] Speaker 1 (automatic): um hm
[02:07] Diego: ok jumping into cache types — prefix cache is best when you have repeated prefixes or fixed prompts; KV (they sometimes call session cache) stores decoder KV state per session which helps long multi-turn convos with big context.
[02:28] Tom: which one gives more cost saving for us? our convos average 7 turns, many reuse system prompts.
[02:38] Diego: generally KV/session cache reduces compute on generation by reusing KV cache for repeated tokens — very helpful for long contexts and for latency. prefix cache is lighter and cheaper to store but requires more cache-hits on prefix strings. In your traces i saw a 28% repeated-prefix rate which is promising for prefix caching.
[03:04] Maya: the term 'KV cash' showed up in the notes — is that different?
[03:09] Avery: that's a transcription thing — it's KV cache. sorry.
[03:13] Sara: walk me through a concrete scenario — we have 10k QPS at peak, 70% are short queries, 30% multi-turn. what should we expect?
[03:25] Diego: (brief pause) ok, i'll sketch two configs: hosted with aggressive batching + prefix cache, and dedicated with KV session caching plus moderate batching. aggressive batching on hosted can push per-token cost down ~18-25% but increases p99 tail; prefix cache reduces token count for repeated prompts possibly another 10-20% depending on hit-rate.
[03:52] Diego: for dedicated with KV caching, because GPU is isolated we can keep smaller latency variance — KV cache tends to reduce generation compute by up to 40% on long convos in our sim, bringing cost way down while keeping p99 low.
[04:10] Tom: sim — can you run that against our traces?
[04:14] Diego: yes, that was my ask — we ran a sample earlier but for a thorough result we'll need the 48-hour trace. we'll run both configs and output a delta table.
[04:26] Maya: any caveats re: TTL or cache invalidation?
[04:29] Diego: TTLs are important. for prefix cache we recommend 12–72 hour TTLs depending on prompt churn; too long and you risk stale outputs. KV caches are per-session, sometimes evict after inactivity like 30–60 minutes depending on memory. we can tune eviction and slot counts.
[04:50] Sara: what about the memory footprint for KV? we anticipate many concurrent sessions.
[04:54] Diego: good point — KV stores are memory-heavy. Our console's optimizer suggests shard counts and autoscale memory buffers; in dedicated you can increase memory per GPU node. the econ model includes memory cost for KV retention.
[05:11] Avery: i pulled an example cost sheet — i'll screen-share the rough sheet after this — it compares tokens, model choice, cache hit assumptions and batching configs.
[05:22] Maya: can you talk about batching policy — we've been conservative because of real-time requirements.
[05:27] Diego: sure. continuous batching groups in-flight requests to the same model for a micro-batch; you tune max latency and concurrency. example: with a max-wait 20ms and concurrency 64 you get higher batch sizes and lower per-token cost, but at the expense of additional queuing time. for your p95 target 200ms it's workable, but p99 depends on worst-case queuing plus model decode time.
[05:55] Tom: any quick rules of thumb?
[05:58] Diego: start with conservative max-wait of 10–20ms and ramp concurrency. monitor p95/p99 in the console. also use smart routing to send free-form long convos to dedicated pools.
[06:12] Sara: you mentioned model variants — we saw mention of smaller quantized models in the docs. where do they fit?
[06:18] Avery: quantized models lower per-token compute; good for short queries and lower-latency needs. Combine them with prefix cache and you might run cheap model for most traffic and fall back to larger model for high-crit flows. that's a routing policy in Redwood.
[06:33] Speaker 2 (automatic): uh huh
[06:36] Diego: another point — cache warmup and cold starts: when you deploy a new model or change prompts, expect a transient increase in cost and latency until caches warm. that's where prefetch/prefix priming helps.
[06:52] Tom: prefetch — are you talking about background priming of KV states?
[06:56] Diego: two flavors: prefix prefetch (precompute responses for expected prefixes) and session prefetch (prime KV for likely next-turn tokens). both require tradeoffs: prefetching increases compute and storage but reduces tail latency during bursts.
[07:12] Maya: any security flags with KV cache? storing session state — is that PII risk?
[07:18] Diego: KV stores only model activation states, not raw user text by default; still, we recommend encryption in transit & at rest (KMS) and RBAC for access. Dedicated/Private gives you control to keep all state within your VPC. we'll share the security pack.
[07:34] Sara: how do you calculate hit-rate in the console? we want confidence intervals.
[07:38] Diego: the Optimize console estimates hit-rate from historical traces — it reports low/expected/high scenarios. it also simulates cost delta under batch/concurrency settings. we'll include CI bands in the sim output.
[07:52] Avery: i'm going to show a hypothetical table (Avery screenshares).
[07:56] Avery: row A: hosted + prefix cache + conservative batching — cost per 1M tokens = $X (placeholder) with p99 ~420ms. row B: dedicated + KV cache + moderate batching — cost per 1M tokens = $Y, p99 ~260ms. difference driven by cache hit rates and reserved GPU economics.
[08:23] Tom: can you put numbers for our 10k QPS peak?
[08:27] Diego: yes — at 10k QPS peak if you maintain 30% KV hit and 28% prefix hits you reduce billed tokens by about 35% in our sim and get ~25% lower cost on dedicated vs hosted for sustained month. but peak autoscale costs still matter.
[08:46] Maya: curious about fallback policies if cache misses spike.
[08:50] Diego: in the console you can configure fallbacks: route to a cheaper model variant or to a different region. also can use graceful degradation policies: reduce max tokens, synthesize shorter responses.
[09:03] Sara: how invasive are the runtime changes? our infra team worries about integrating new SDKs.
[09:08] Diego: integration is minimal for API users — same REST/SDK, you toggle cache settings in Optimize or via route config. for Private on-prem installs you may need extra network/firewall rules for the control plane.
[09:23] Tom: latency sampling — how granular is the tracing? we need per-token breakdowns.
[09:28] Diego: Redwood Console has token-level and phase-level breakdowns (queue, compute, decode). we can preserve logs in your KMS-backed storage for audits.
[09:40] Maya: quick objection — our security team is skeptical of hosted because of logs and multi-tenancy.
[09:46] Avery: understood — that's why Dedicated/Private and contract language around data residency exist. we also offer audit logs, field-level encryption, SSO/SAML, and SOC2. we'll send the security brief.
[09:58] Sara: are there customers similar to us who've done KV-heavy POCs? any refs?
[10:02] Avery: yes, we've done POCs with a couple of retail and health customers — i can share anonymized case notes.
[10:09] Tom: can the sim model session stickiness? we are worried about sessions bouncing across nodes.
[10:15] Diego: yes, session affinity is supported — you can pin sessions to nodes to keep KV warm. there's an availability tradeoff if a node dies but you can set replication factors.
[10:29] Maya: replication for KV — that increases cost, right?
[10:32] Diego: correct — replication improves availability but increases memory and storage usage. the console will show cost impact.
[10:42] Speaker 3 (automatic): mm hmm
[10:46] Diego: i'm going to walk through a short sim we ran earlier (Diego shares link: https://redwood.example/sim/ff-20270831-quarry-sim) — it's anonymized.
[10:58] Diego: scenario 1: hosted + prefix cache assumptions: 28% prefix hits, batch max-wait 20ms, concurrency 64. outcome: token reduction 20–30%, p99 380–420ms. scenario 2: dedicated + KV cache: KV hit 30%, replication 1, batch concurrency 48, outcome: token reduction 35–45%, p99 240–300ms.
[11:26] Tom: those p99 numbers are promising. what's the engineering effort for dedicated?
[11:31] Avery: typically a few weeks to provision capacity and route traffic; Private on-prem longer because of infra. POC with contrained traffic can start in 1–2 weeks.
[11:42] Maya: oh there's a question about storage TTL for prefix entries. are they stored on disk or memory?
[11:49] Diego: prefix cache entries can be in-memory or persisted depending on config. in dedicated we often keep an LRU in memory with disk fallback. size and TTL depend on the uniqueness of prefixes.
[12:02] Sara: what about model switching for cost — operate cheap model then escalate?
[12:06] Diego: exactly — dynamic routing: route low-confidence or short responses to quantized models and escalate to larger models on fallback. this is in routing policy and the console shows expected cost/latency impact.
[12:20] Maya: does Redwood's Optimize automatically suggest these routes?
[12:23] Avery: yes, Optimize proposes recommendations based on your traces and desired SLOs, like 'use quantized small model for X% of traffic' and 'enable KV for sessions > N tokens'.
[12:37] Tom: any gotchas with telemetry or tracing overhead?
[12:40] Diego: tracing adds small overhead; we sample aggressively for tail analysis and let you control retention. sampling config is in console.
[12:51] Sara: can we limit the console's access to certain teams? we're worried about exposure.
[12:55] Diego: RBAC is supported. you can restrict dashboard views and logs per team, integrate with SAML/SSO.
[13:05] Avery: i see a chat question — "what's the expected unit delta for our example?" Diego?
[13:10] Diego: for your 10k QPS peak, ballpark: hosted $A per 1M tokens, dedicated $B per 1M tokens with sustained commit. the sim will give exact numbers; i'd expect 20–30% saving on dedicated when KV is effective.
[13:25] Maya: we're also evaluating Anthropic for some gen tasks — how does Redwood compare?
[13:30] Avery: competitively — Redwood focuses on serving economics and operational control; others may have model-capability advantages. our differentiation is runtime optimizations, caching, and unified routing across hosted/dedicated/private.
[13:46] Tom: security follow-up — can you sign an NDA and do a deeper architecture review with our security folks?
[13:51] Avery: yes — we can onboard legal and sign an NDA, and schedule a security deep dive.
[13:58] Diego: quick detail on batching: continuous batching works best when you have bursty arrival patterns. if your traffic is extremely spiky with tiny QPS intervals, the benefit drops. the console's sim takes arrival distribution into account.
[14:16] Sara: what about cold-starts for KV when we have a new model version?
[14:20] Diego: cold-starts require re-priming. our rollout patterns (canary and staged) allow you to warm caches by mirroring a small percentage of traffic or by scheduled prefetch jobs.
[14:33] Maya: are there metrics for cache correctness and stale hits? we need to audit outputs.
[14:38] Diego: yes, we log cache-hit/miss events and can store snapshots for a given time range. you can build audits, and we can redact sensitive fields.
[14:48] Tom: let's talk follow-up POC scope — what would you recommend?
[14:52] Avery: POC scope: 1) run 48-hour trace sim; 2) small dedicated pool sized for peak 10-20% traffic; 3) enable KV for sessions > N; 4) measure p95/p99 and cost delta; 5) security review. timeline 2–4 weeks.
[15:09] Maya: fine. can you also include a cheaper-canary route so we don't risk user experience?
[15:13] Diego: yes, we usually suggest a canary that routes 5–10% of traffic initially with circuit-breakers.
[15:20] Speaker 4 (automatic): okay
[15:23] Sara: a small detail — TTL ring sizing for prefix cache, how is eviction chosen?
[15:28] Diego: eviction uses LRU with configurable buckets; ring sizing is based on estimated unique prefixes per hour. we'll run numbers with your trace.
[15:38] Tom: how do we handle GDPR/data subject requests? if logs contain snippets should we be worried?
[15:45] Avery: we support data retention policies and can redact or delete logs on request; Private deployments let you control archival.
[15:54] Maya: price sensitivity — i'll ask product & finance to review your pricing.
[15:58] Avery: perfect. we'll send a dedicated-pricing sheet and the SOC2/security pack by EOD tomorrow.
[16:05] Diego: i'll queue the sim to run with your trace when Tom uploads. deliverable will be a CSV with scenarios and a dashboard link.
[16:13] Sara: can you include a mid-range scenario (moderate cache hit) plus best and worst case?
[16:17] Diego: yes — low/med/high hit-rate bands.
[16:20] Tom: any final notes re: model quantization tradeoffs?
[16:23] Diego: quantization is a big enabler but watch hallucination/quality — tie quality tests to your evals. Redwood Optimize can flag regressions against prompt sets.
[16:36] Maya: that helps. i'd like to bring our security lead into the next call.
[16:40] Avery: absolutely. we'll invite them to the security deep dive.
[16:44] Sara: ok next steps recap?
[16:47] Avery: recap: 1) avery sends pricing + security pack; 2) tom uploads 48h trace; 3) diego runs sims and returns dashboard; 4) schedule poc kickoff week of 9/6 with infra and security.
[17:04] Tom: sounds good.
[17:07] Maya: thanks all.
[17:10] Avery: thanks everyone. we'll follow up in email with links and dates. bye.
[17:14] End of recording.
